result.reasoning:
I reproduced the stratum construction exactly from the three named files (30 strata, mean treatment 0.26944, mean per-stratum control 0.09772, obs +0.17173) and then ran six attacks. Five of the six failed to dent it; the sixth kills the magnitude, not the effect.

ATTACK 1 — STRUCTURAL OPPORTUNITY / SHIFTING DENOMINATOR. This was my best shot and it failed cleanly. `data/cost-index-events.json` has wildly heterogeneous history spans: 63 slugs start 2001 (~25y) but 27 start 2024/2025 (span.years as low as 1.2). Two ingredients whose price histories barely overlap CANNOT share an episode, so if substitute partners systematically had longer-overlapping spans than controls, the whole effect would be a coverage artifact. There IS an asymmetry — mean structural ceiling (fraction of the anchor's events whose ±6wk window intersects the partner's span) is 0.9667 for treatment vs 0.8938 for controls. But conditioning it away does nothing: restricting BOTH arms to full-overlap pairs only (23 strata) gives +17.58pp, p<5e-5 — slightly LARGER. Opportunity-normalising (v/ceiling) gives +16.94pp, p<5e-5. Not a span artifact.

ATTACK 2 — DENOMINATOR ASYMMETRY IN k/n. cavg is (k_ab/n_a + k_ba/n_b)/2, so a small-n partner can only score 0 or 1 and would inflate. Mean n_b = 5.567 vs mean n_c = 5.737; treatment has 2 of 30 partners with n<=2, controls 9 of 251. The asymmetry runs slightly the wrong way for the finding and is far too small to matter.

ATTACK 3 — SELECTION ON THE DEPENDENT VARIABLE. The decisive question is whether `subSlug` was populated preferentially where co-movement existed. It was not. In `data/ingredient-depth.json` the substitute rows carry authored culinary fields (`name`, `ratio`, `worksFor`, `failsFor`) and `subSlug` is a mechanical name→slug resolution: exactly ONE of the 162 null-subSlug rows has a name matching a corpus slug (olive-oil→butter), and 29 populated subSlugs point OUTSIDE the 100-slug priced corpus (swiss-chard, parsnip, fennel, portobello-mushroom). If resolution had been outcome-driven it would have stopped at the scoreable set. The `hedge` field is strictly downstream — non-null for 71/71 rows where both members are anchors — and is correctly excluded from the treatment definition.

ATTACK 4 — PSEUDO-REPLICATION / EFFECTIVE n. The real dependency structure is worse than the caveat's "23 distinct anchors": connected components of the treatment graph give only 14 independent units, and ONE component of size 10 contains all the lettuce and cabbage strata (bok-choy, butter/green-leaf/iceberg/red-leaf/romaine lettuce, cabbage, napa-cabbage). Drawing one stratum per component, 200 random draws: median diff +13.2pp, median p=0.0010, p95=0.0130, only 1% of draws exceed p=0.05. Cluster bootstrap over the 14 components (10k reps): 95% CI [+10.1pp, +21.0pp], ratio 2.76x with 95% CI [2.07x, 4.12x], 0 of 10,000 reps at or below zero. The sign of the effect is not in doubt even at honest effective n.

ATTACK 5 — OUTLIER AND CLIQUE DEPENDENCE. Jackknife range is +14.72pp (drop chicken-breast/thigh, the most influential single stratum) to +18.34pp — no single observation carries it. Drop the 6 lettuce×lettuce strata: +10.93pp, p=0.00065. Drop the top-5 treatment values: +9.76pp, p=0.0003. Drop the 13 same-commodity-variety pairs entirely (lettuce, chicken, cabbage, squash, pepper, pork, tomato varieties) and the remaining 17 genuinely cross-commodity substitute pairs still give +9.85pp, p=0.00055. This is the answer to the "it's just the same commodity reported twice on the same AMS line" objection, and it holds.

ATTACK 6 — MULTIPLICITY. The engine enumerated 38 hypotheses (`counts.hypotheses` = 38, outcomes 7/25/6). The primary statistic sits at z = 5.30 (obs 0.17173, null mean 0.000121, null sd 0.032391), normal-approx p ≈ 6e-8; Bonferroni at 38 leaves 2e-6. Fine. Autocorrelation is differenced out by construction — the anchor a is held fixed across treatment and controls, so the anchor's own temporal event density (the thing `coMovementBaseRate` in scripts/lib/cost-events-analysis.mjs warns about) cancels within stratum.

WHAT DOES NOT SURVIVE: the number 2.8x. Every de-clustered, de-outliered, drop-rule-restored variant lands near +10pp, not +17pp — restored drop rule +12.11pp, one-per-anchor +10.30pp, drop lettuce +10.93pp, drop top-5 +9.76pp, cross-commodity-only +9.85pp, one-per-component median +13.2pp. The cluster-bootstrap 95% CI on the ratio is [2.07x, 4.12x]. "2.8x" is a point estimate from the most favourable of the many analysis paths, published bare. The magnitude-free sign test is also much weaker than the headline: 19 wins, 7 losses, 4 ties, one-sided binomial p = 0.0145 — i.e. the permutation's tiny p is being carried by the size of a handful of values, not by a broad tilt across strata.

Two presentation defects a numerate reader will catch. (a) The revisedClaim's decisive split reports 32 same-category + 6 cross-category = 38 pairs, but its headline reports the 30-pair primary design — two different designs in one paragraph with no signal that the denominator changed. On a site where every number must re-derive, that reads as an arithmetic error. (b) "chicken breast to chicken thigh sits at 0.92" quotes two significant figures off (5/6 + 5/5)/2, from six and five detected episodes — and it is simultaneously the single most influential stratum in the whole result. Given the events builder caps at TOP_N = 6 (scripts/build-cost-index-events.mjs line 51) and 65 of 80 anchors sit at exactly n=6, the measure only moves in steps of 0.167 and no value here deserves two decimals.

None of this is fatal. The effect exists, is large, is not a span artifact, is not circular with the repo's own `hedge` verdict, and holds after the same-commodity clique is removed. It is the advertised precision that fails.

I hunted for a mundane mechanism that reproduces +17.17pp / 2.76x without any substitute→entanglement relationship. Four candidates, three dead, one that survives and forces the headline down.

DEAD 1 — coverage/vintage/density artifact. Anchors have wildly different histories (data/cost-index-history.json: 61 of 80 span 2001–2026 at ~1,313 weekly points, but chicken-breast/chicken-thigh/whole-chicken/whole-turkey are 200 points 2022-08-29→2026-06-22 and bok-choy is 129 points 2024–2026). Two short-window items get their 6 events forced into the same 4-year box while long-window controls scatter theirs over 25 years — a pure density lift. I re-placed each neighbor's events uniformly on its OWN date grid (counts and direction multiset preserved, 400 draws/pair, ±6wk window per data/cost-index-events.json params cohortWeeks=6): expected treatment 0.0575 vs expected control 0.0477, diff +0.0098. That is 5.7% of the observed gap. Not the mechanism.

DEAD 2 — plain seasonality. build-cost-index-events.mjs uses a centered ±26-week median baseline (line ~46, BASE_WIN=26), which folds annual seasonality in but not sharp region-transition weeks, and substitutes share growing calendars. Month-preserving null (same month-of-year, random year within the item's own span): treatment 0.0715 vs control 0.0486, diff +0.0229 — 13% of the gap. Not the mechanism.

DEAD 3 — treatment selected on the outcome. data/ingredient-depth.json has 162 of 296 substitute sub-rows with subSlug:null, and `hedge` is populated iff subSlug is. If the author had assigned subSlug preferentially to high co-movers the whole result would be manufactured. Only 11 null rows have a `name` that resolves to an existing anchor; 6 are scoreable and they average 0.361 — HIGHER than the 0.269 treatment mean (red-leaf↔romaine 0.833 and iceberg↔romaine 0.667 are both sitting excluded). The omissions run the wrong direction to fake this. This partly retires the finding's own caveat #7.

SURVIVES — same reported commodity under different variety/cut names. Controls are category-matched but declared substitutes are excluded from the control pool by construction, so within a category the treatment arm is systematically lettuce×lettuce / chicken-part×chicken-part while the control arm is systematically lettuce×brassica. 11 of the 30 strata are within-lettuce, within-chicken or within-cabbage; they average 0.4015 against 0.1130 controls (+0.2885), and the remaining 19 average 0.1930 vs 0.0889 (+0.1041, 2.17x, p=0.0003, 20k permutations). Under a stricter botanical grouping (also removing cherry-tomato/tomato, yellow-squash/zucchini, acorn/butternut, the peppers, collard/kale, green-onion/leek, pork-belly/pork-shoulder) n=11 remains at +0.1020, p=0.0043. So the relationship is real but roughly 60% of the published magnitude comes from pairs that are barely two ingredients: green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce print the IDENTICAL carton price in 385 of 1,312 common weeks (29.3%), r=0.939, median ratio exactly 1.000 — they are effectively one quoted line on the LA terminal report. Mean identical-print rate is 1.62% for treatment pairs vs 0.63% for controls.

The showpiece number is the weakest link. chicken-breast↔chicken-thigh at 0.917 against a stratum control mean of 0.033 contributes (0.917−0.033)/30 = 0.0295, i.e. 17% of the entire +0.1717 headline, from one pair. Shared reporting per se is NOT the mechanism, which is worth stating because the finding's caveat overweights it: controls drawn from the anchor's own terminal market average 0.1384 (n=115) vs 0.0908 (n=136) cross-market — a real ~5pp lift on the control baseline — but treatment pairs get no benefit from sharing a market (0.2675 same-market n=19 vs 0.2727 cross-market n=11), and the market-matched subset still runs +0.1887 (n=11). Provenance gap worth naming even though it did not kill: `grep -rn "subSlug" scripts/` returns zero hits. The treatment variable has no committed generator, was written by hand or by an uncommitted workflow (ingredient-depth.json `generated: 2026-07-11`, the same day cost-index/co-movement.json was written), and cannot be reproduced from the repo.

A ranked table of undirected pair entanglement scores IS the retired object. Worse, ADR-015 uses as its worked example of the asymmetry that must be preserved: "chicken-breast→thigh 5/6 is not thigh→breast 5/5." The operative sentence — "the standard trade advice 'swap to the cheaper one' is systematically weaker as a hedge" — is about what an operator PAYS. `cost-index/menu-pricing.json` `note` states the contract: "Every band is a wholesale reference read against each ingredient's own baseline window — never a delivered or retail price." That caveat is required and absent.

3) Forecast posture. `menu-pricing.json` note: "Descriptive of the tracked record, never a forecast." result.reasoning:
The statistics are clean; the originality is not. Three strikes, any one of which is close to fatal on this lens.

1) THE SITE ALREADY PUBLISHES THE CONCLUSION, VERBATIM. /home/user/potentially-profitable/open/recalls/index.html line 331 (generated by scripts/build-open-recalls-page.mjs line 211) ships this sentence live: "A reference lookup, not a consequence — a recall is never a price signal." The same page carries "never joined to a price" 10 times, and build-open-recalls-page.mjs lines 8-9 and 531-541 enforce a structural no-price guard ("There is NO price token anywhere on this page (asserted at build)"), with a build-time assertion that fails if a "$" appears. scripts/lib/recall-roster.mjs lines 30-33 injects the same line onto every one of the ~100 EN+ES ingredient pages: "shown as co-occurrence, never a cause, never joined to a price." The revised claim's payload sentence — "a recall notice carries no advance warning of an ingredient's price departure" — is a restatement of muntin.digital's own published doctrine. Publishing it as a discovery is publishing evidence for a sentence the site already asserts. That is a methods footnote for /open/recalls/, not a finding.

2) THE EXTERNAL LITERATURE SETTLED THIS 15-20 YEARS AGO, AND IT SAYS THE TESTED DIRECTION IS THE WRONG ONE. USDA ERS published the market response to exactly this class of event: the 2006 spinach E. coli outbreak (ERS Amber Waves, June 2007; Arnade/Calvin/Kuchler, Rev. Ag. Econ. 31(4):734-750, 2009) measured a $202.5M fall in spinach sales against a $141.9M rise in lettuce — a demand shock that pushes the implicated commodity's price DOWN and substitutes UP. A published VAR study covers cantaloupe 2008, spinach 2006 and tomato 2008 against domestic shipments, imports AND prices. On the meat side, Marsh/Schroeder/Mintert (Applied Economics 36(9), 2004) found recall elasticities small relative to price and income effects. The finding's primary test is UP-episodes only — the direction the literature already predicts should be null. The code (conf[6].code) filters `if x["direction"] == "up"` for both A and the 5,000-iteration null; the any-direction number (11/362 = 3.04%) is reported with NO null of its own, and there is no down-only test at all. So the one direction prior art actually predicts was never tested against chance, and the substitute-side effect — the part that is both established and operator-relevant — was not touched, despite cost-index/co-movement.json sitting in the same repo.

3) THE POOLING DESTROYS THE EVENT CLASS PRIOR ART SAYS MOVES MARKETS. data/food-recalls.json has 718 notices across 315 events with a MEDIAN OF 1 NOTICE PER EVENT (max 70). The literature is about publicized multistate outbreaks that strip product from the national market — the Thomson onion Salmonella Newport event (1,127 illnesses, 48 states, nationwide distribution) is one of exactly two such events curated in cost-index/events.json, alongside Jensen Farms cantaloupe 2011 (pre-window). The finding pools that with ~200 single-notice firm-level lot recalls. Its only severity stratification is Class I only (4/192 = 2.08%), and Class I is an FDA HEALTH-HAZARD class (426 of 718 notices), not a distribution-scale or publicity proxy — a single-lot undeclared-allergen recall from one bakery is Class I. So the null is a dilution artifact of the specification, and nobody ever hypothesized that a 200-case allergen recall moves an AMS terminal-market series. The finding's own surprisingness rating of 2 is generous; the honest rating is 1.

SEPARATELY, ON ACTIONABILITY — it is thin in both directions. The implied action is "don't read your recall feed as a price feed," but operators respond to recalls with lot-checks, pulls and substitution, not procurement timing, so the myth being busted may not exist in the population. Worse, the tempting reading — "recalls don't affect my food cost" — is precisely what the corpus cannot support: the caveats concede delivered price is absent and no public series carries it. And the detection ceiling forecloses the actionable band entirely: data/cost-index-events.json params are topN=6 and floorPct=20, i.e. only each ingredient's six largest LIFETIME moves clearing a 20% departure from a centered ±26-week normal, over a median 25.2-year span; 18 of the 55 tested ingredients have zero post-2020 up-episodes and could never register a hit. An operator re-prices on a 5-10% move. The finding answers "does a recall predict a once-in-a-decade wholesale spike?" (no) and is structurally silent on every magnitude a kitchen would act on. Minimum detectable effect is 1.84x the null — nothing finer.

WHAT WOULD SURVIVE. Not this claim. The same corpus one line of code away could test the direction the literature predicts (down-episodes with their own null) and the substitute channel via co-movement.json — either confirming the ERS demand-shock result on a new corpus or genuinely contradicting it. That would be a finding. This is a validation of house doctrine, dressed as a discovery.
